payload.title: Korean Traditional Wedding Customs Explained
payload.audience: Couples in their 30s interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget
payload.reader: An Australian couple in their 30s with a generous budget, often with a Korean partner or Korean-Australian parents, who want to understand what the families will expect (the ham, yedan and yemul, a wedding hall ceremony followed by the pyebaek, hanbok, chukuigeum), honour the customs with confidence, and decide whether to marry in South Korea (Smartraveller: exercise normal safety precautions, updated 12 October 2026) or bring the customs into a wedding at home.
payload.goal: Read the free Wedded Wonderland digital magazine (primary CTA); secondary, in-context invitation to speak with a Wedded Advisor placed after the 'for Australians' section.
payload.angle: Most lists show a hanbok and a pyebaek photo and stop there. We walk through a Korean wedding in the order families live it today: the ham and the yedan and yemul exchanges before the day, the Western-style ceremony in a wedding hall that most couples hold, then the pyebaek with the groom's family (jujubes, chestnuts, the bride carried on the groom's back) and chukuigeum at the reception desk, with the full jeontong honrye, its wooden wedding geese and the wonsam or hwarot and samogwandae explained for couples who want the traditional ceremony itself. Garment and ceremony names follow Korea's museums and the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture; everything else is living practice that varies by family, region and faith. We close with what Australians need, as Smartraveller and the Australian Embassy in Seoul word it, and how Korean-Australian couples hold a pyebaek at home.
must_include: One early framing line, said once: customs vary by family, region and faith, and most Korean couples today hold a Western-style ceremony with a short traditional ceremony (pyebaek) after

About 10 to 12 numbered sections in wedding order: the ham; yedan and yemul; the modern wedding hall format; the traditional ceremony (jeontong honrye) and its steps; the wooden wedding geese; hanbok (wonsam or hwarot, samogwandae); the pyebaek; jujubes, chestnuts and carrying the bride; chukuigeum; UNESCO (only if confirmed); for Australians
Korean terms in Revised Romanisation as sources give them, hangeul only where a source gives it, inline definitions
Yedan, yemul and chukuigeum described with no amounts or price ranges
No meaning or origin stated as fact unless sourced (geese, jujubes and chestnuts); 'often told' at most once

Section for Australians: Smartraveller 'Exercise normal safety precautions' (updated 12 October 2026, as at November 2026), DMZ tensions as worded, rainy and typhoon seasons, 90-day entry and K-ETA exemption to 31 December 2026, Australian Embassy Seoul for CNI or affidavit and notarial, 'Getting married overseas', district office registration or questions to ask including any fees, same-sex recognition line as worded; Seoul and Jeju as places couples choose; Korean-Australian weddings at home
FAQ of 5 to 7 questions with no amounts (what is a pyebaek, what to wear as a guest, what is chukuigeum, can we hold a pyebaek in Australia, is a traditional ceremony legally binding)

Internal links: /destinations/asia; Japanese and Chinese traditions drafts; /the-dos-and-donts-of-asian-destination-weddings; natural cross-link to /trending/korean-stars-married-october-2026; /expert-advice/wedding-traditions pillar

tradition_plan.note: Planner (wedding-planner-sme) runs batch A and batch B in parallel, scratch folders 02-research/batch-a and 02-research/batch-b, 15 min HARD by the clock, save after every 3 facts, no extra sourcing rounds, never retry a declined call. Preferred sources: Korea Tourism Organization, National Folk Museum of Korea, National Museum of Korea, Academy of Korean Studies (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture), Korean Cultural Centre Australia, UNESCO, Britannica, the V&A, academic sources. Never competitor wedding sites, vendor blogs or Wikipedia. Unsourced customs are written as living practice with no meaning or origin as fact and no [[VERIFY]] marker; 'often told' at most once per post. Source gaps go in the run report only (authority rule).
